column2: ECB publishes Survey of Professional Forecasters results for Q4 2026
column3: The European Central Bank released the results of its Survey of Professional Forecasters for the fourth quarter of 2026.
column4:
The European Central Bank (ECB) has published the results of its Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF) for the fourth quarter of 2026. The SPF collects professional forecasters' expectations for euro area inflation, GDP growth and unemployment. The release provided here contains no specific figures.

The survey is closely watched as a gauge of private-sector inflation expectations and their anchoring relative to the ECB's target. Depending on its content, it could influence market pricing of the ECB policy path, with possible spillovers to euro area rates and EURUSD. Higher-than-expected inflation expectations would likely be read as hawkish and supportive of the euro. Softer expectations could reinforce bets on easier policy. Any direct impact is likely to be modest, since the SPF is one input among several for policymakers.

Global crude oil refinery inputs fell by 4.8 million barrels per day (b/d) in the second quarter of 2026 (2Q26), or 6%, following the start of conflict in late February in the Middle East, according to data from Kpler. ECB wage tracker suggests slightly higher wage growth in first three quarters of 2027 compared with the full year of 2026
column3: The European Central Bank's wage tracker points to slightly higher wage growth in the first three quarters of 2027 than over the full year of 2026.
column4:
The European Central Bank published an update to its wage tracker. It indicates slightly higher wage growth in the first three quarters of 2027 than across the full year of 2026. The release gives no specific figures beyond this direction.

Modestly firmer wage growth could support euro-area household incomes and consumption. It could also add some upward pressure on services inflation. If policymakers see that pressure as persistent, markets might price a somewhat less accommodative ECB rate path, which could lend mild support to the euro. Because the change is described as slight, any effect on rates and FX would likely be limited.
